caseno: Appeal from Original Order Nos. 217 & 218 of 1977.
lawyer:
S. R. Paul with Khalilur Rahman ------ For the Appellants. 
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with A. K. Mainul Huq ------ For the Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Dacca Match Factory Ltd  ------ Plaintiff-Appellant (in Appeal Nos. 217 & 218 of 1977)
Vs.
Bangladesh Match Company Ltd. Principal  ------ Defendant-Respondent (in both the Appeals)
full_judgment:
M. H. Rahman J.—These two appeals have arisen out of the order dated 20.4.77 passed by Mr. Anisul Haque Choudhury, Additional District Judge, Special Court No. 2, Dacca in Title Suit No. 4 of 1977 rejecting the plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction and the plaint. They have been heard together and this judgment will dispose them of. 

 2. The plaintiff, Dacca Match Factory Limited, a company registered under the Companies Act, now placed under the control and management of Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation, has been manufacturing and selling safety matches for last twenty years under the trade mark Horse Brand registered in Pakistan on 27. 10. 58 and renewed for 15 years with effect from 27. 10. 65; after the liberation of Bangladesh the plaintiff's trade mark was registered summarily under Registration No. 8207 in class 34 under the Bangladesh Trade Marks (Invalidation and Summary Registration) Order, 1973; the plaintiff's Horse Brand' safety matches are of superior quality and has been enjoying a considerable reputation and goodwill in the market; that, defendant No.1, Bangladesh Match Company, has infringed the plaintiff's registered trade mark by manufacturing and selling safety matches using the mark of a horse with the design, appearance and general set-up so nearly resembling the plaintiff's trade mark that it is likely to deceive or cause confusion in the course of a trade and to unwary converters, and hence the plaintiff brought this suit for permanent injunction and for damages for infringement of registered trade mark. 

 3. After filing the suit the plaintiff filed an application for a temporary injunction. Defendant No.1 entered appearance and filed written objection denying the material allegation made in the plaint and contended that the Pakistan Match Factory Ltd. the predecessor/of defendant No.1 used 9 kinds of trade marks including the disputed one namely, Chand Ghora (Crescent with a device of horse and stars). From 29.5.73 to 17.6.74 the defendant's Match Factory was under the Bangladesh Fertilizer, Chemical and Pharmaceutical Corporation. On 19.11.74 the Government of Bangladesh released the concern in favor of M/s. M. M. Ispahani the defendant's Chand Ghora safety matches are of superior quality and are sold at a retail price of 15 paisa each match box against those of the plaintiff which are of inferior quality and sold at 20/25 paisa each match box; the defendant's trade in ark' 'Chand Ghora' is quite different from that the plaintiff; and there are various other trade marks used on safety matches having picture of horse namely '3 horses' 'horse and arrow and stars' 'horse -with ladder' and 'horse with stripes' etc.- the defendant has applied before the Registrar of Trade Marks for registration of their trade mark 'Chand Ghora' an order of temporary injunction would cause serious dislocation and irreparable loss to The defendant and the plaintiff's prayer for the injunction should he rejected as the defendants have been using the mark 'Chand Ghora' for a long time since January 1971, Defendant No. 1 further contended that the suit was not maintainable and was liable to be rejected under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 4. F. M. A. No. 217 of 1977 is directed against the order rejecting the plaint. The learned Additional District Judge held that the plaintiff's company having been placed under the management and control of Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation under the President's Order No. 27 of 1972 read with Ordinance No.XXI of 1976. Sub-article (2) of Article 10 makes it clear that none for the Corporation under which the plaintiff's Company has been placed can sue or be sued for the alleged infringement of right and the plaintiff - Company is not permitted to sue in its individual character. Relying on the decision of Chowmuhani College Vs. Md. Ismail Hossain (1974) 26 DLR 10 the learned Judge rejected The plaint under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code. 

 5. Mr. S. R. Paul, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant has submitted that the learned Judge erred in rejecting the plaint outright without allowing the plaintiff to adduce evidence in this regard. He has further contended that under the President's Order No. 27 of 1972 industrial enterprises, either nationalized or placed under the control and management of a corporation have got their distinct personalities as they have not been merged in the Corporation! The Corporation has been created to perform the function of general supervision and control ever the industrial enterprises placed under it; besides, as the plaintiff obtained the registration of the trade mark and is The owner of the trade mark in question it is in fitness of things that the plaintiff itself should bring action for any infringement to its right. Again, the Corporation having been brought on record as defendant No. 2. the competency of the plaintiff to sue through its manager could not be questioned in law. 

 6. Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for defendant No.1, has contended that the plaintiff-company has got no power or authority to sue in its own name. H has, however, conceded that as the question of maintainability was examined in connection with an application for temporary injunction there was no occasion for production of necessary evidence before the Court whether the Manager of the plaintiff's firm had authority to sue on behalf of the plaintiff firm. 

 7. It is difficult from pleadings of the parties, submitted in connection with the application for temporary injunction, to find out whether plaintiff-firm was authorized by the Corporation to sue in its own name or whether the Manager was authorized to sue in The name of the plaintiff-firm on behalf of The Corporation or whether there was any Government direction which has altered or modified prevision of clause (b) of Article 8 of the President's Order 27 of 1972. Clause (b) Article 8 reads as follows: 

 9. F. M. A. 128 of 1977 directed against the rejection of the petitioner's prayer for temporary injunction. The learned Judge has found that the visual and phonetical dissimilarities between the plaintiff's 'Horse Brand' and the defendant's 'Chand Ghora' were so obvious that any ordinary man would find and notice the striking differences; the plaintiff's trade mark is know as 'Horse Brand' while the defendant's trade mark is known as 'Chand Ghora'; the picture of horse has been used in labels of different safety match manufacturing concerns; the defendant has been using their marks since January, 1971 and the plaintiff-company who was so long silent in raising any objection could not suffer any irreparable loss while the defendant-company is likely to be adversely affected by the temporary injunction, and the plaintiff has failed to make out a prima facie case of infringement of trade mark warranting an order of temporary injunction. 

 10. Mr. S. R Pal has pointed out that the learned Judge instead of finding out minor details to show difference between the two labels ought to have found That they were identical and, there were striking similarities in color, design, sizes and get-up of the labels and running posture of the horse so that ordinary unwary customers who are not literate, would be deceived and the defendant's label would be passed as that of the plaintiff in the market. He has further contended that the differences between 'Ghora' and 'Chand Ghora' are hardly distinguishable on cursory view, and that the phonetical difference between 'Ghora' and 'Chand Ghora' is of consequence in deciding a case of infringement of registered trade mark; and as the plaintiff has a vested right in The registered trademark if had a vested interest in the general get-up in the trade mark and any attempt to copy the same or to put similar labels which are likely to create confusion can be resisted by a suit for permanent injunction. As the defendant is manufacturing matches with other trade marks such as 'Scale Brand', 'Crescent', 'Deer', 'Tiger, 'BMC' and ' 5 Stars', as disclosed in its written objection, any order of temporary injunction restraining, The defendant company would not cause any adverse effect like alleged loss of employment to its employees. In support of this contention Mr. S. R. Pal cited to us "Thomas Dear and Sons (India) Limited Vs. Prayag Narain" A.I.R. 1940 Privy Council 86. In this case dispute arose between two users of mark of elephant, one for cigarette and pipe tobacco and another for tobacco products used with lime end betel. Mr. Pal has drawn our attention to the following observation made in this case. 

 13. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has submitted that as the plaintiff has failed Jo make out a prima facie case of infringement of its trade mark the learned District Judge has rightly rejected the prayer for temporary injunction. He has cited to us M/S. Pharmapak Laboratories Ltd. Vs. Deputy Registrar, Trade Mark, (1967) 19 DLR 99; Master Thread Ball Works Vs. H. A. Karim, (1969) 21 DLR 388 and the Signer Company Vs. Ahmed Ali, (1969) 21 DLR 415 and Pakistan Medical Supplies Vs. M/s. Farben Fabriken Bayer AIG. (1969) 21 DLR 945 to demonstrate that the Courts have considered the visual and phonetics differences between the contending marks like "Alkacit and 'Alkaseltzer', 'Master Tailor Thread Brand and Master Thread Ball Works, Sagar and Singer and 'Bayer' and 'P.M.S.' 

 14. Mr. Ahmed also referred to Firm Mohanlal Harprassad Vs. Firm Lai Mohammad reported in A.L.R. 1962 (Madhya Pradesh) 237. In this case it was held that the granting of a temporary injunction would not be in accordance with law where The only similarity between the labels of the two parties Was in "the picture of a cow and in the use of four colors, there was no proof of any attempt on the part of the defendant to pass off its goods as the goods of the plaintiff, the sphere of market for the goods of both parties was different and the defendant had been using his labels much before the registration of the plaintiff's trade mark. 

 15. In an action for infringement of a registered trade mark the Court must of necessity enquire whether the defendant's trade mark is identical or deceptively - similar to the plaintiff's trade mark. Even in The case cited by Mr. Pal, "Thomas Dear and Sons (India) Ltd. Vs. Prayag Narain" it was observed 

 The learned District Judge has rightly considered the dissimilarities between the two tables. On the plaintiff's labels it is written as “বাংলাদেশ প্রস্তুত” and “দি ঢাকা ম্যাচ ফ্যাক্টরী লিঃ” "whereas on the defendant's label it is written only “বাংলাদেশ ম্যচ কোঃ লিঃ”। On the plaintiff's label if is written on the left hand side “আদ্রতা and  রোধক” on The right hand side, but on defendant's label it is written “আদ্রতা  রোধক”   together on the left hand side, and “অতি উত্তম” on the right hand side. The expression “অতি উত্তম” is not in the plaintiff's label. On Plaintiff's label there is a star on each Conner of the label and on the defendant's label there is a flower on each corner. On the plaintiff's label "Horse" shown in a motion running towards right. On the plaintiff's label there is simply horse but on the defendant's label there is a device of horse combined with a big prominent crescent and seven stars scattered on it. It appears that manufacturers of safety matches in the country have got a fancy for horse as trade mark. There are several other safety matches with horse marks selling in the market. The defendants mark is known at 'Chand Ghora'. This is clear from the cash memo dated 7-2-77 obtained by the plaintiff in its test purchase. The cash memo and other correspondences filed by the defendant clearly show that the defendant's product is known as "Chand Ghora" in the business community. 

 16. For some time both the plaintiff and the defendant were under general supervision and control of the Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation., The question of infringement did not appear to have been raised during that time. The plaintiff has, however, stated in the affidavit-in-reply that the defendant started using the horse brand only in late 1976. 

 17. From the pleadings of the parties and annexures submitted by them and examination of the plaintiff's trade mark as a whole, and not merely a particular part of it, namely, the horse mark, the defendants' label does not appear to be identical to the plaintiffs' trade mark and there is no confusion at least amongst the dealers of safety matches as to the respective identities of the two contending marks. As the plaintiff has failed to make out a prima facie case of infringement' it is not entitled to an order of injunction. Where there is no prima facie case of the defendant's using improperly the plaintiff's registered trade mark, injunction will not issue in an infringement action. The facts of R. Johnston & Co. Vs. Archibald Orr. Euring & Co. Law reports (A. C.) Vol. 7, page 219 and of Fullwood Vs. Fullwood, Chancery Division Vol. IX, 176 have got no relevance in the instant case. 

 18. Our views in this appeal are to be understood in relation to the injunction matter only. Whether the defendant has infringed the plaintiff's registered trade mark and whether the plaintiff is entitled to damages for such alleged infringement, these matters are to be examined and decided in the suit. 

 In view of the above, we allow F.M.A. No. 217 of 1977 and remit the case to the trial Court for trying the issue of maintainability along with other issues that may be raised in the suit. F.M.A. No. 218 of 1977 is dismissed. We affirm the impugned order refusing to grant temporary injunction to the plaintiff. The connected civil Rule is discharged, and the ad interim order of injunction is vacated. There will be no order as to costs.
